Berakhot No.1: A Brief History of Jewish Time
sheets.summary: The beginning chapters of Masekhet Berakhot, the first tractate of the Talmud, are rather occupied with the concept of time. And reading through these chapters, it seems clear that the Rabbis of the Talmud thought of and recorded time in quite a different way than we do now. Hear David Zvi Kalman, PhD discuss the imprecision and perfectness of timekeeping from the Talmud to the 21st century. Listen here: https://podfollow.com/interleaved-a-talmudic-podcast/episode/61f2749506a079c9ba17526af2cf2c29fcd614b0

en.title: When God Hears Kaddish
en.prompt: Kaddish, or at least elements of it, go back at least to the talmudic period. The Babylonian Talmud in tractate Berakhot recounts a story of a rabbinic sage who learns how God reacts to the Jewish people when they praise God’s name with the words of kaddish.

he.title: יתגדל ויתקדש שמו הגדול
he.prompt: תפילת הקדיש היא בקשה להגדלת שם ה' בעולם. ישנם כמה סוגים של תפילת קדיש המובדלים בתוספות שונות, אך בכולם נמצא עיקר הקדיש המכונה גם "חצי קדיש".

description.en: Kaddish is an Aramaic prayer that declares praise of God. Its four main variants punctuate Jewish prayer services, marking the end of each section and its conclusion. It describes God's holiness and greatness and calls for the recognition of God's eternal rule over all of mankind. It is only recited in the presence of a prayer quorum and is further adapted for different contexts, including burials and to mark ritually the conclusion of a significant body of learning, a siyyum.
description.he: הקדיש היא תפילה הכתובה בארמית ונאמרת בסיום התפילה או במהלכה. בזמן חיבור התפילה הייתה הארמית שפה מדוברת ומובנת יותר מהעברית. התפילה מתארת את קדושת האל וגדולתו וקוראת להכרה של כלל האנושות במלכות האל.

description.en: Mourner's Kaddish is the practice of mourners to recite Kaddish at the beginning and end of prayer services and other occasions. This declaration of their faith in God, is thought to help the souls of the dead to whom they dedicate their recitation.
description.he: קדיש יתום הוא קדיש הנאמר על ידי אבלים בתחילת התפילה ובסופה וכן בזמנים אחרים. הקדיש הוא הצהרת אמונה בקב"ה, שעל פי המסורת עוזרת לנשמות הנפטרים שעליהם נאמר הקדיש.

description.en: [The Shema](https://www.sefaria.org/Siddur_Ashkenaz%2C_Weekday%2C_Shacharit%2C_Blessings_of_the_Shema%2C_Shema?lang=bi), Judaism's most famous prayer, is actually not a prayer at all. Rather it is a declaration of God's unity and other central doctrines of Judaism. It involves reciting three passages from the Torah, one of which is interrupted by another ancient phrase, the origins of which are outside the Bible.

description.en: Time is a concept that appears from the very beginning of the Torah, as the world's creation unfolds over seven days, each of which is divided into evening and morning. Sources throughout the Jewish textual tradition discuss how God and people sanctify time, different ways of relating to the passing of time, how time governs the performance of commandments, and how to make the most of one's time.

The Babylonian Talmud in tractate Berakhot references I Chronicles 27:34 to discuss the notable figures in King David's administration, including Ahitophel.

description.en: Prayer is a central aspect of Jewish life and features prominently throughout the Jewish textual tradition. Biblical characters commune with God, expressing their gratitude, distress, and desires. [Liturgical works](https://www.sefaria.org/texts/Liturgy) contain set prayers to be recited at regular schedules, while works of Jewish thought stress the importance of integrating personal connection into prayer.
description.he: על פי המסורת, תפילה היא חלק מרכזי בעבודת ה' ומלווה את היהודי באופן יומיומי, בתפילות ציבור ובתפילות יחיד, בשבת ומועד וגם בימי חול. אנשי כנסת הגדולה קבעו את החובה להתפלל שלוש פעמים ביום. תפילות קבועות אלה הפכו להיות בין השאר, תחליף לקורבנות המקדש. נוסחי התפילות המרכזיות נקבעו על ידי חכמי המשנה ובכל דור נוספו עוד תפילות לסדר התפילה הקבוע.

description.en: Nighttime serves as the setting for pivotal moments in biblical history, including God’s [covenant of the pieces](https://www.sefaria.org/Genesis.15.12?ven=hebrew|Tanach_with_Ta%27amei_Hamikra&lang=bi&with=all&lang2=en) with Abraham, Jacob’s [wrestling](https://www.sefaria.org/Genesis.32.23?ven=hebrew|Tanach_with_Ta%27amei_Hamikra&lang=bi&with=all&lang2=en) with the angel, the [plague](https://www.sefaria.org/Exodus.12.29?lang=bi&with=all&lang2=en) of the firstborn, and the [splitting of the sea](https://www.sefaria.org/Exodus.14.20?ven=hebrew|Tanach_with_Ta%27amei_Hamikra&lang=bi&with=all&lang2=en). Rabbinic sources emphasize the special value of Torah study at night, teaching that a “[thread of kindness](https://www.sefaria.org/Chagigah.12b.8?lang=bi&with=all&lang2=en)” accompanies those who engage in it, and many communities observe the custom of studying Torah throughout the night of Shavuot. Sources of Jewish thought and liturgy also portray the night as a particularly fitting time for introspection, devotion, prayer, and revelation.

In Judaism, priests are believed to be the descendants of [Aaron](https://www.sefaria.org/topics/aaron?tab=sources). In the Bible, they are charged with doing the ritual work in the [Mishkan](https://www.sefaria.org/topics/mishkan?tab=sources) and later the Temples, under the leadership of a [high priest](https://www.sefaria.org/topics/high-priest?tab=sources). In Temple times, priests were also entitled to certain gifts and portions of sacrifices. Today, some people of priestly descent recite a special blessing in the synagogue and are careful to avoid contact with corpses, among other responsibilities and restrictions. The Hebrew word for priest is kohen.

Moses was the greatest prophet in the biblical tradition. Raised by the daughter of Pharaoh in the Egyptian royal family, after he fled Egypt, he married [Tzipporah](https://www.sefaria.org/topics/tzipporah1), the daughter of a Midianite priest, [Yitro](https://www.sefaria.org/topics/yitro). After an encounter with God at the burning bush, God sends Moses back to lead the Israelites out of slavery and to [Mount Sinai](https://www.sefaria.org/topics/mount-sinai) to received the Torah and then through the desert to the promised land. Tragically, he is not allowed to enter the land.
description.he: משה היה גדול הנביאים במסורת המקראית. הוא גדל בבית פרעה, ברח ממצרים ונשלח לשם בחזרה על ידי אלוהים כדי להוציא את בני ישראל מעבדות ולהביאם לארץ המובטחת. משה קיבל את התורה בהר סיני כדי למסור אותה לבני ישראל. הוא נפטר לפני כניסת העם לארץ המובטחת.

description.en: Elijah — known as Eliyahu in Hebrew — was a prophet in the [book of Kings](https://www.sefaria.org/I_Kings?tab=contents) who championed the worship of God during the reign of King Ahab, a time when many were turning to the worship of the Canaanite god, Ba'al. Elijah performed miracles to prove the superiority of the God of Israel. He never died but was taken to the heavens in a fiery chariot. He reappears in the Talmud to address difficult questions, and a cup is put out for him as part of the Passover seder. It is also believed that his return will signal that the arrival of the messiah is imminent.
description.he: אליהו הוא נביא בספר מלכים בתקופת מלוכתו של אחאב. בתקופה זו פנו רבים לעבודת האל הכנעני בעל. אליהו השתמש בניסים ובמופתים להוכחת עליונותו של אלוהים. אליהו לא מת אלא נלקח לשמים במרכבה של סוסי אש.

en.title: God's Lament in Exile
en.prompt: Rabbinic sources describe God as mourning the exile of God’s people. The Babylonian Talmud details Rabbi Yossi’s encounter with God’s lament.
en.ai_context: The Talmud describes God bewailing the exile.
en.ai_prompt: Even in exile, God shares in the pain and sorrow of the Jewish people, highlighting a profound emotional connection. The Babylonian Talmud in tractate Berakhot presents a narrative where a Heavenly voice expresses God's lamentation over the destruction of the Temple and the exile of His children.

description.en: There were two Jewish Temples, or *battei mikdash* (singular: *beit mikdash*) that stood in ancient Jerusalem. The first was built by [King Solomon](https://www.sefaria.org/topics/king-solomon?tab=admin) and destroyed by the Babylonians in 586 BCE, and the second was built in the late sixth century BCE with the blessing of the Persian Empire and was later destroyed by the Romans in 70 CE. These Temples were the central site of Jewish sacrifice and pilgrimage while they stood. The destruction of these holy Temples was tragic, traumatic, and completely transformational for Jews and Judaism. The Temples and the service of God that took place there are described extensively in Jewish texts, as are their destructions and practices surrounding how they are mourned to this very day.
description.he: בית המקדש נבנה בירושלים בידי שלמה המלך כדי להחליף את המשכן ואת המזבחות האחרים בארץ וכדי לשמש מרכז לחיים היהודיים ולעבודת הפולחן היהודית. החורבן הסופי של המקדש מתואר באריכות במקורות חז"ל.

description.en: Death is a concept discussed throughout Jewish literature, beginning with the second chapter of the Torah, in the context of the world's creation. Sources throughout the generations grapple with the concept of mortality, responding emotionally to death, and the laws and customs that surround death and mourning.
description.he: מושג המוות עולה ברחבי הספרות היהודית, החל מהפרק השני של התורה בבריאת העולם. מקורות לאורך הדורות מתחבטים במושג המוות, בתגובה הרגשית אליו ובהלכות ומנהגים המקיפים את המוות והאבל.

description.en: In Hebrew, the same word is used to refer both to “song” and “[poem](https://www.sefaria.org/topics/poetry).” The [Hebrew Bible](https://www.sefaria.org/texts/Tanakh) includes songs appearing at pivotal moments in the narrative, including the [Song of the Sea](https://www.sefaria.org/topics/song-of-the-sea1) after the crossing of the [Red Sea](https://www.sefaria.org/topics/red-sea), the Song of [Ha’azinu](https://www.sefaria.org/topics/parashat-haazinu) at the end of the journey through the wilderness, and the [Song of Deborah](https://www.sefaria.org/Judges.5) after a victory in the book of Judges. Songs (or poems) also make up books such as the [book of Psalms](https://www.sefaria.org/Psalms) and [Song of Songs](https://www.sefaria.org/Song_of_Songs). Jewish [liturgy](https://www.sefaria.org/texts/Liturgy) include religious songs composed throughout Jewish history, sometimes called piyyutim. Jewish communities in different times and locations have developed a diversity of traditions of secular and religious singing.

God is central in traditional Jewish texts. God [utters the world into existence](https://www.sefaria.org/Genesis.1.1?lang=bi&with=Translations&lang2=en) from the outset of Genesis, and Rambam, in the opening to his halakhic masterpiece, Mishnah Torah, explains that belief in God is the [foundation of all foundations](https://www.sefaria.org/Mishneh_Torah%2C_Foundations_of_the_Torah.1.1?lang=bi&with=all&lang2=en). Countless Jewish sources discuss God's essence, the constraints of using human language to describe a transcendent Being, and how people are to develop relationships with God.

Dogs first feature in the Torah in the book of Exodus, when, during the final plague in Egypt, [God ensures](https://www.sefaria.org/Exodus.11.7?lang=bi&with=all&lang2=en) that not even a dog would snarl at the people of Israel. Later in the same book, the Torah instructs that certain meat that is forbidden for human consumption be [given to dogs](https://www.sefaria.org/Exodus.22.30?lang=bi&with=all&lang2=en). Rabbinic sources explore the connection between these two references to canines. In other biblical, rabbinic, halakhic, and mystical texts, dogs feature in many negative contexts — for example, they are often depicted as feeding on corpses and as dangerous to humans. Still, other sources highlight positive qualities of dogs, such as their ability to sense the unseen and their helpfulness to people who need it.

The *sanhedrin* ("assembly") was a legislative and judicial assembly of either 23 or 70 elders, existing at both a local and central level in the ancient Land of Israel.

Sleep features from the outset of the Bible, as God [casts](https://www.sefaria.org/Genesis.2.21?lang=bi&with=all&lang2=en) a deep sleep on Adam when God creates Eve. Other biblical texts incorporate sleep as well – as a [step](https://www.sefaria.org/Judges.4.21?lang=bi&with=all&lang2=en) in a plot, as a metaphor for laziness or spiritual disengagement, or as a [precursor](https://www.sefaria.org/Genesis.28.12?lang=bi&with=all&lang2=en) to divinely-inspired dreams. Rabbinic and kabbalistic texts later discuss the spiritual significance of sleep and dreams, as well as halakhic questions related to sleep, such as the parameters for the obligation to sleep in the sukkah. Jewish liturgy incorporates prayers to be recited upon going to sleep and upon waking up in the morning.

Terumah is the tithe, or heave offering, taken from produce grown in the land of Israel and given to the [kohanim, or priests](https://www.sefaria.org/topics/priesthood?sort=Relevance&tab=notable-sources).
description.he: תרומה היא מתנה מקודשת הנלקחת מן היבול החקלאי בארץ ישראל וניתנת לכוהנים.

description.en: While demons appear in a few episodes in the Hebrew Bible, they are more prominent in talmudic and kabbalistic literature. Jewish texts tell stories of demons, analyze their nature, discuss how to avoid them, and explain how fear of demons shapes some Jewish practices.

Tisha B’Av, the ninth day of the Hebrew month of Av, is a fast day and the saddest day on the Jewish calendar. Among other historical tragedies, it commemorates the destruction of the First and Second Temples in Jerusalem in 586 BCE and 70 CE, respectively. One fasting abstains from food and other physical pleasures, reads the biblical book of Lamentations, and observes mourning customs.
description.he: תשעה באב, החל בט' באב, הוא צום בן 25 שעות שיוצא בדרך כלל ביולי או אוגוסט. יום זה, המצוין על-ידי הימנעות מאכילה, שתייה, רחצה, יחסי מין ומלבושי עור, הוא יום של אבל על חורבן בית המקדש הראשון והשני בירושלים.

description.en: Tisha B’Av, the ninth day of the Hebrew month of Av, is a fast day and the saddest day on the Jewish calendar. Among other historical tragedies, it commemorates the destruction of the First and Second Temples in Jerusalem in 586 BCE and 70 CE, respectively. One fasting abstains from food and other physical pleasures, reads the biblical book of Lamentations, and observes mourning customs.
description.he: תשעה באב, החל בט' באב, הוא צום בן 25 שעות שיוצא בדרך כלל ביולי או אוגוסט. יום זה, המצוין על-ידי הימנעות מאכילה, שתייה, רחצה, יחסי מין ומלבושי עור, הוא יום של אבל על חורבן בית המקדש הראשון והשני בירושלים.

description.en: [The Shema](https://www.sefaria.org/Siddur_Ashkenaz%2C_Weekday%2C_Shacharit%2C_Blessings_of_the_Shema%2C_Shema?lang=bi), Judaism's most famous prayer, is actually not a prayer at all. Rather it is a declaration of God's unity and other central doctrines of Judaism. It involves reciting three passages from the Torah, one of which is interrupted by another ancient phrase, the origins of which are outside the Bible.
description.he: קריאת שמע היא תפילה ידועה השגורה בפי עם ישראל והיא כוללת שלושה קטעים מפסוקי התורה ומשפט אחד שאינו מן התנ"ך. המילים של קריאת שמע הן הצהרה על ייחוד האל, אהבתו וקבלת עול מצוות. קריאת שמע היא מצווה מהתורה הנאמרת פעמיים ביום, בתפילת שחרית ובתפילת ערבית. רבים שמתו על קידוש השם קראו את קריאת שמע לפני מותם כהצהרה על אמונתם.

description.en: Blessings are declarations of acknowledgement to God about His greatness, His gifts or His connection with the Jewish people via the commandments. While they follow several formats, they all include the key phrase, "Blessed are You, O Lord!"
description.he: הברכות הן הצהרות של הכרה בגדולת האל על מתנותיו ועל הקשר המיוחד שלו עם העם היהודי דרך המצוות. לברכות נוסחים רבים ושונים, אך משותפת להם הפתיחה "ברוך אתה ה', אלוקינו מלך העולם".

description.en: The destruction of the Temple can refer to the destruction of either of the two Temples that stood in Jerusalem in the ancient period. The First Temple, built by King Solomon, as described in the book of I Kings, was destroyed in 586 BCE by Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon. The Second Temple, built approximately 70 years after the destruction of the first, was destroyed in 70 CE by the Roman Empire.
description.he: חורבן בית המקדש, או בקיצור ״חורבן הבית״, הוא מושג המתייחס לשני אירועים היסטוריים - חורבן בית המקדש הראשון בשנת 586 לפני הספירה על ידי נבוכדנצר מלך בבל, וחורבן בית המקדש השני בשנת 70 לספירה על ידי טיטוס - קיסר האימפריה הרומית. לעיתים, המושג ״חורבן הבית״ מתייחס באופן נרחב יותר לאיבוד עצמאותו המדינית של עם ישראל בארצו בתקופות אלו. בעקבות החורבן, תיקנו חז״ל 4 ימי תענית: עשרה בטבת - בו התחיל המצור על ירושלים בבית ראשון, י״ז בתמוז - יום ביקוע חומות ירושלים, תשעה באב - הצום העיקרי בו חרבו שני בתי המקדש וצום גדליה - בו נרצח גדליה בן אחיקם אשר היה הנציב היהודי בירושלים לאחר חורבן בית ראשון.

description.en: "Safek" is a term originating from Rabbinic literature and is not found in the Bible itself. In legal contexts, when uncertainty arises, approaches vary depending on whether the commandment in question originates from the Torah or from Rabbinic sources.
description.he: הספק ההלכתי מתעורר כאשר האדם אינו יודע באיזו דרך פעולה לנקוט במקרה מסוים. מצב שכזה אינו נזכר בתורה ומופיע לראשונה בספרות חז"ל. דרך הפעולה שיש לנקוט במקרה של ספק בסוגיה מסוימת משתנָה בהתאם למקורה של ההלכה הקשורה לאותו הספק – הלכה שמקורה בתורה או בחז"ל.

description.en: The struggle to make ends meet and provide for material needs appears from the beginning of the Torah, as figures like Abraham and Sarah confront famine. Later books of the Torah establish a series of commandments designed to support the poor: farmers must [leave](https://www.sefaria.org/Leviticus.19.9-10?lang=he&aliyot=0) the corners of their fields and gleanings for the needy, debts are [canceled](https://www.sefaria.org/Deuteronomy.15.2?lang=bi&with=all&lang2=he) every seven years, and the people of Israel are repeatedly commanded to [open their hands](https://www.sefaria.org/Deuteronomy.15.8?ven=hebrew|Tanach_with_Ta%27amei_Hamikra&lang=bi&aliyot=0) to those in need. Stories of the poor and their plights and successes abound in rabbinic literature, which also delves into the details of operating communal charity systems. Throughout the Jewish textual tradition, sources explore the meaning of poverty, debating whether it should be understood as a divine response to wrongdoing or as a refining condition that cultivates humility and simplicity.

Rabban Gamliel (II) was a tannaitic sage in the first and second centuries CE. He was the first to serve as *nasi* (leader of the *[Sanhedrin](https://www.sefaria.org/topics/sanhedrin?tab=admin)*) after the destruction of the Second Temple and worked to strengthen the Jewish community and leadership in the post-Temple era. Rabban Gamliel occasionally acted in ways that involved publicly shaming other rabbis, which led to pushback and his temporary deposition.
description.he: רבן גמליאל היה בנו של רבן שמעון בן גמליאל. הוא היה נחוש לרכז ולהעצים את כוח הסנהדרין ביבנה כדי למנוע את התפוררות העם היהודי לאחר חורבן בית המקדש, בשאיפה להנחות ולנתב את התסיסה האינטלקטואלית בזמנו. כמה מעמיתיו הבולטים התנגדו למאמציו, והוא אף הושעה מהנשיאות למשך תקופה מסוימת.

description.en: Bread is considered a staple of life in the Jewish textual tradition. Biblical figures offer bread to their guests as a marker of hospitality, and the sacred showbread plays a role in the rituals of the Tabernacle and Temple. [Many laws](https://www.sefaria.org/Jerusalem_Talmud_Challah.1.6.3?lang=bi&with=all&lang2=en) govern the preparation, baking, and consumption of bread. Bread is unique in that its consumption necessitates reciting the full [Birkat HaMazon](https://www.sefaria.org/topics/birkat-hamazon?tab=admin) (Grace After Meals).
description.he: הלחם נחשב למצרך יסוד במטבח העם היהודי. הלכות רבות מתארות כיצד יש להכינו ולאוכלו, וכן הוא המזון היחיד שאכילתו מחייבת ברכה מלאה אחריה (ברכת המזון).

description.en: Wind plays a role from the very beginning of the Torah, as a [wind from God](https://www.sefaria.org/Genesis.1.2?lang=bi&vside=The_Contemporary_Torah,_Jewish_Publication_Society,_2006|en&with=Translation%20Open&lang2=en) sweeps over the waters in the opening verses of Genesis. Winds are critical in other prominent biblical stories as well, such as when the wind helps split the Red Sea, brings [quail](https://www.sefaria.org/Numbers.11.31?lang=bi&aliyot=0) to the desert, or helps revive the dead in Ezekiel's [Valley of Dry Bones prophecy](https://www.sefaria.org/Ezekiel.37.1?lang=bi&with=all&lang2=en). In rabbinic texts, the rabbis discuss how wind affects areas of halakhah, such as under what conditions someone is [liable for damages](https://www.sefaria.org.il/Bava_Kamma.60a.4?lang=bi&with=all&lang2=en) caused by wind and what types of wind the [sukkah walls](https://www.sefaria.org.il/Sukkah.23a.4?lang=bi&with=all&lang2=en) must withstand. The word "wind" is also used in the context of the directions north, east, south, and west and their spiritual significance, as well as to refer to a person's [spirit](https://www.sefaria.org.il/Pirkei_Avot.4.4?ven=hebrew|Torat_Emet_357&lang=bi&with=all&lang2=en) or a moral force.

en.title: After the Destruction of God's Home
en.prompt: The destruction of the two Temples, first by the Babylonians and then centuries later by the Romans, signified the loss of God's dwelling place among the Jewish people on earth. The Babylonian Talmud in tractate Berakhot describes how, after the destruction, the divine presence was forced into exile but lingers in other Jewish communal spaces.
en.ai_context: Destruction and exile: This story in the Talmud tells of God’s mourning for the destruction of God’s home, and God’s consolation finding a home in synagogues and study halls.
en.ai_title: The Divine Presence in Our Homes
en.ai_prompt: The concept of home is not only a physical space but also a spiritual one, where the divine presence can dwell. The Babylonian Talmud, in tractate Berakhot, explores the idea of God's home, its destruction, and the subsequent exile of the Jewish people, while also highlighting the new 'homes' God finds in synagogues and study halls.

description.en: In Jewish tradition, having a home means that one has a place in which to fulfill such obligations as [welcoming guests](https://www.sefaria.org/topics/welcoming-guests?sort=Relevance&tab=notable-sources), placing [mezuzot](https://www.sefaria.org/topics/mezuzah?tab=notable-sources) on their doorposts, and commemorating the [destruction of the Temples](https://www.sefaria.org/topics/destruction-of-the-temple?tab=notable-sources). Jewish tradition also uses the idea of home as a metaphor, likening a wife to a home and imagining God as dwelling in God’s homes of the [Tabernacle](https://www.sefaria.org/topics/mishkan?tab=notable-sources) and, later, the [Temples](https://www.sefaria.org/topics/beit-hamikdash?tab=notable-sources). Peace in one's home ([shalom bayit](https://www.sefaria.org/topics/shalom-bayit?tab=notable-sources)) is also a priority.

[The Talmud](https://www.sefaria.org/texts/Talmud/Bavli) is the textual record of generations of rabbinic debate about law, philosophy, and biblical interpretation, compiled between the 3rd and 8th centuries and structured as commentary on the [Mishnah](https://www.sefaria.org/texts/Mishnah) with stories interwoven. The Talmud exists in two versions: the more commonly studied Babylonian Talmud was compiled in present-day Iraq, while the Jerusalem Talmud was compiled in Israel.

en.title: King David's Midnight Devotion
en.prompt: King David's profound devotion to rising at midnight to serve God is a subject of discussion in the Gemara's tractate Berakhot. The text cites Psalms and Proverbs to reconcile apparent contradictions and offers various rabbinic interpretations regarding King David's practice.
en.ai_prompt: King David's dedication to rising at midnight demonstrates an extraordinary level of devotion and commitment. The Gemara in Berakhot discusses King David's practice, citing Psalms and Proverbs, and offers various rabbinic interpretations to resolve the apparent contradictions.

description.en: Praise of God involves expressing gratitude and admiration directly to Him in diverse situations and contexts. While the book of Psalms contains numerous instances of such praise, similar expressions can also be found in other books of the Bible and subsequent religious texts.
description.he: תהילת אלוקים הוא הצהרת הערכה כלפי הקב"ה במגוון מצבים והקשרים. הצהרות כאלה מצויות באופן מרוכז בספר תהילים אך גם נפוצות בספרים אחרים בתנ"ך ובטקסטים דתיים מאוחרים יותר.

description.he: ההגדרות המדויקות של מה נחשב לדירה, כלומר בית ראוי למגורים, חשובות לשלל ענייני הלכה. לדוגמה, הגודל המינימלי של דירה הוא גם הגודל המינימלי של סוכה כשרה, ורק בתים בגודל הזה ומעלה חייבים במזוזה.
description.en: In Jewish law, it’s important to understand what constitutes an abode (dirah). For example, a sukkah (temporary hut) must be large enough to be considered an abode, and the same is true in order for a structure to require a mezuzah (parchment enclosed in a case on a doorpost).
